evidence.evidenceSnippet: UCL staff and students can now access Microsoft Copilot. Microsoft Copilot is a safer generative AI tool than using the consumer-oriented generative AI services, provided you log in with your UCL credentials.

Microsoft Copilot is our approved GenAI tool because of its enhanced data protection. This tool is a more secure and safer alternative to other GenAI services. Read about how you can use Microsoft Copilot easily and safely.
If you sign into Microsoft Copilot with your UCL credentials you can be confident that:
your prompts, questions and results are protected
the chat data is not saved
Microsoft has no eyes-on access.
This means no one can view your data and your data is not used to train the AI models.

Microsoft Copilot is grounded in data from the public web and provides verifiable answers with citations, along with visual answers that include graphs and charts. It is designed in line with Microsoft’s AI principles.

tools.description: Formative academic writing, structure and referencing feedback; not substantive assessment text or academic credit.
tools.howToObtain: Access through UCL Moodle. Available 24/7 with unlimited uses for current UCL students.
tools.costToUser: Not verified in the reviewed evidence.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Studiosity can review your work and give you feedback to help improve the structure, language, spelling and grammar, and use of sources in your writing. This service is available 24/7 and there is no limit to the number of times you can use it.

This means that, unlike other AI tools, you can use Studiosity with confidence that it is supporting your learning. Studiosity, uses a ‘closed system’ AI, so your work remains your own and will not be used to train AI.
All current UCL students can access Studiosity via Moodle, where you'll also find frequently asked questions and links to further resources

UCL is the Controller of your personal data for the purposes of providing academic skills support. Studiosity Pty Ltd (Studiosity) acts as a Processor when providing services on behalf of UCL. Additionally, Studiosity acts as an independent Controller for data collected directly from you to manage your user account and platform improvements.

Your personal data is processed by Studiosity in Australia and the United States. To ensure your data receives an adequate level of protection, these transfers are governed by the UK Approved International Data Transfer Addendum.†ico.org.uk
* Service Content: Submitted academic drafts for feedback, "Connect Live" session transcripts (including audio recordings), and chat histories.

We have put in place appropriate security measures to prevent data loss or unauthorized access. This includes AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2+ encryption in transit, and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for administrative access. We retain your data only as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes of the service or as required by the UCL Records Retention Schedule .

claims.claimText: For Caltech Bi 1 (2026), generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and Colab AI) are prohibited unless an assignment explicitly instructs students to engage with them on a per-problem basis.

You may not use generative AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Copilot, Colab’s built-in AI) in this course.

title.en: Confirm the course and data conditions before using AI.
title.zh: 使用 AI 前，确认课程与资料条件。

scope.en: In HSS, use AI only as explicitly allowed by the instructor in the course materials; assume other uses are disallowed. Bi 1 rules are course-specific. Admissions rules concern applications; tool access does not approve assessment or sensitive-data use.
scope.zh: HSS 仅允许教师在课程材料中明确准许的 AI 使用方式；未明确准许的用途应视为不允许。Bi 1 规则仅适用于该课程。招生规则针对申请；工具可用不代表作业或敏感资料获准。

do.en: Check the exact assignment and audience.
do.zh: 核对具体作业要求及适用对象。

do.en: Follow disclosure instructions and applicable exceptions.
do.zh: 遵守披露要求及适用例外。

do.en: Check data classification and tool mode.
do.zh: 核对资料分类与工具模式。

dont.en: Do not infer assessment permission from tool access.
dont.zh: 不要把工具可用当作作业许可。

dont.en: Do not infer sensitive-data approval from no-training terms.
dont.zh: 不要用不训练承诺推定敏感资料获准。

dont.en: Do not extend a course or publisher rule to the entire university.
dont.zh: 不要把课程或出版社规则推广到全校。

Therefore, in general the use of GenAI in generating content, including text and figures that can be seen as interpretation of research finding is not allowed. claims.text: For HKU Faculty of Law assessed work, an educative response may involve rewriting and resubmission with a penalty. evidence.quote: When a teacher is satisfied that submitted work contains plagiarism or involves the misuse of generative and other AI tools, and that an educative response (usually involving re-writing and re-submission with a penalty) is not appropriate, then an academic response will be adopted, pursuant to which the plagiarized work may be given a mark of zero or a reduced mark. claims.claimText: In general, HKU does not allow GenAI-generated text or figures that constitute interpretation of research findings. Unavoidable use should be limited in scope, acknowledged and reported.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: 27. In most academic disciplines, interpretation of data in a research study can be regarded as a core element of intellectual and original contribution of scientific research. The researcher is ultimately accountable for all the claims made in the study. Therefore, in general the use of GenAI in generating content, including text and figures that can be seen as interpretation of research finding is not allowed. If the use of the GenAI tool is unavoidable, it should be limited in scope and duly acknowledged and reported. E. Use of GenAI tools for research output / publication

claims.claimText: HKU does not accept use of GenAI in peer review of research outputs or funding applications because of integrity and confidentiality concerns.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: 32. The use of cloud-based commercial AI platforms has the potential to inadvertently disclose the content of papers or funding applications under review, thus violating the integrity and confidentiality of the established double-blind peer review process. claims.claimText: For HKU Faculty of Law assessed work, an educative response may involve rewriting and resubmission with a penalty. Where this is not appropriate, an academic response may reduce the mark or give zero. Misuse may also be referred as a disciplinary offence; this is not automatic expulsion.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: When a teacher is satisfied that submitted work contains plagiarism or involves the misuse of generative and other AI tools, and that an educative response (usually involving re-writing and re-submission with a penalty) is not appropriate, then an academic response will be adopted, pursuant to which the plagiarized work may be given a mark of zero or a reduced mark. In addition, the matter may be treated as a disciplinary offence (just like the case of cheating during an examination) and referred to the University’s Disciplinary Committee under Statute XXXI of the University’s Statutes and the Disciplinary Committee Regulations.
evidence.snippetLocation: Academic and disciplinary responses; normalized_extracted_text; quote characters 2805–3441; part 1/1.

topics.title: 课程作业
topics.summary: NTU’s 2025 statement generally permits assignment AI use, with teacher prohibitions for pedagogical reasons. Current Library guidance requires module instructions and explicit permission for extensive use.
topics.scope: Dated institutional statement and current Library guidance; internal full teaching policy not obtained.

claims.text: NTU’s dated 24 June 2025 statement says GenAI is generally permitted in assignments, but professors may prohibit it for specific pedagogical reasons communicated to students. Students are expected to declare use and how it was used, and remain responsible for accuracy and citations. This is a dated institutional statement, not the complete current internal teaching policy or permission for every assessment.

evidence.quote: NTU’s policy is that in general, students are allowed to use Gen AI in their assignments. Many Schools across STEM and non-STEM disciplines, in medicine, and at NIE, are already using AI as part of learning. Students are expected to declare any use of AI, and how they are being used. When using AI, students are ultimately responsible for the content generated. They must ensure factual accuracy and cite all sources properly. Some professors may prohibit Gen AI for certain assignments for specific pedagogical reasons. In such cases, the reason for disallowing it is clearly communicated to students.
evidence.title: Comment on the use of AI in education | NTU Singapore

claims.text: NTU Library instructs students to disclose AI-tool use in their submissions and follow their module’s AI-use policy and instructor guidance. evidence.quote: When using AI for assignments (e.g., grammar checks, copyediting, or idea generation), adhere to the specific guidelines set by your instructor, as expectations may vary by module and discipline. This may include documenting your AI use, completing a “ Declaration on GAI Use ,” or disclosing AI contributions where required. To uphold academic integrity, you must always provide proper citations for all sources used, including AI‑generated content.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: NTU’s policy is that in general, students are allowed to use Gen AI in their assignments. Many Schools across STEM and non-STEM disciplines, in medicine, and at NIE, are already using AI as part of learning. Students are expected to declare any use of AI, and how they are being used. When using AI, students are ultimately responsible for the content generated. They must ensure factual accuracy and cite all sources properly. Some professors may prohibit Gen AI for certain assignments for specific pedagogical reasons. In such cases, the reason for disallowing it is clearly communicated to students.

claims.claimText: The Harvard Law Graduate Program permits AI queries to clarify exam-relevant concepts while studying, but prohibits queries about exam subject matter during the exam. Pre-writing AI text for incorporation into an exam is not permitted. Instructors may set different rules only when described in writing and communicated to all students. This applies to the Graduate Program policy, not all Harvard courses.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: While preparing for an exam, a student would be permitted to email another person about the subject matter of the exam and/or ask that person to explain a relevant concept. Similarly, while studying for an exam, a student would be permitted to submit a prompt to an artificial intelligence application about topics or concepts relevant to the exam. In contrast, a student would not be permitted to ask either another person or an artificial intelligence application to pre-write text for the student and then incorporate that text into their exam.

claims.claimText: The Harvard Law Graduate Program permits AI queries to clarify exam-relevant concepts while studying, but prohibits queries about exam subject matter during the exam. Pre-writing AI text for incorporation into an exam is not permitted. Instructors may set different rules only when described in writing and communicated to all students. This applies to the Graduate Program policy, not all Harvard courses.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: While preparing for an exam, a student would be permitted to email another person about the subject matter of the exam and/or ask that person to explain a relevant concept. Similarly, while studying for an exam, a student would be permitted to submit a prompt to an artificial intelligence application about topics or concepts relevant to the exam. In contrast, a student would not be permitted to ask either another person or an artificial intelligence application to pre-write text for the student and then incorporate that text into their exam.

Unless otherwise specified by your instructor, it is a violation of the HGSE Academic Integrity Policy to use generative AI to create all or part of an assignment for a course (e.g., a paper, memo, presentation, or short response) and submit it as your own.
Permissible uses of generative AI in HGSE coursework include seeking clarification on concepts, brainstorming ideas, or generating scenarios that help contextualize what you are learning.

basis.evidenceSnippet: Faculty should be clear with students they’re teaching and advising about their policies on permitted uses, if any, of generative AI in classes and on academic work. Students are also encouraged to ask their instructors for clarification about these policies as needed.

All faculty are required to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use in class. Whether students in your course are forbidden from using ChatGPT or expected to explore its limits, a policy helps ensure that your expectations for appropriate interaction with generative AI tools are clear to students.
More specifically, you should post your policy on your Canvas site.

Faculty must get documented permission from students before putting original student content into any generative AI tool, and students should be made aware of the risks of entering their original work into such tools.
No confidential information can be loaded into GAI systems, since there is no expectation of privacy or confidentiality.

HUIT and School IT providers have procured a range of generative AI tools with important contractual protections for use in Harvard work. These include security and privacy protections that ensure the tools are appropriate for use with certain types of confidential data, and assurances that the data entered will not be used to train vendor models.

dimensions.summary: Appropriate personal study and formative use is broadly permitted subject to local rules. Unacknowledged AI-generated content in summative assessment is misconduct; Engineering Triposes have additional conditions.
Summative-assessment and local assessment-brief restrictions apply. This crawl did not establish one universal examination permission rule; check your Faculty and examination instructions.

Unacknowledged summative content is misconduct. Engineering requires declaring preparation use unless the brief says otherwise. General educational advice uses the significant AND unrevised contribution condition.

Educational and research data rules apply in their own contexts. Staff administrative guidance explicitly excludes student learning, assessment and research. Examiners may not upload student work to GenAI.

University Workspace offers Gemini and NotebookLM. Standard Microsoft licences include Copilot Chat at no extra cost for most staff/students; paid M365 integration has account conditions. Access does not grant assessment permission.

RDM framework version 4 requires research data and AI-use considerations across the research community. Its statement that there is no distinct GenAI research policy does not establish unrestricted use.

basis.evidenceSnippet: Examiners across all programmes of study (including Undergraduate, Postgraduate Taught, and Postgraduate Research) are not permitted to upload, copy, or share student work with Generative AI (GenAI) tools and Large Language Models (LLMs).
Examiners may not use tools, such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google Bard, or Microsoft Copilot, to analyse work submitted by students and provide written feedback.
Due to lack of clarity and uncertainty of how these tools use and/or store input data, it is not permitted to share student IP and submitted work without permission from the student.
Where preferred, however, examiners may use these tools to support their own writing in the process of documenting feedback (e.g., consolidating personal notes and rephrasing comments).

The University of Cambridge broadly permits the appropriate use of GenAI tools and related software, however, due to the variety of disciplines and research areas present at the institution, there is need for more nuanced guidance at local levels.

Students are permitted to make appropriate use of GenAI tools to support their personal study, research and formative work. Appropriate use is better defined locally by Department, Faculty, or College depending on the context and you should always check with a member of staff to be sure you know how you are able to use these tools for your education. General guidance for use of GenAI is available as well as specific guidance for assessment-related queries.

basis.evidenceSnippet: If it is necessary and beneficial to use GenAI tools, it is recommended that wherever practicable the University’s licensed GenAI tools, Copilot, Gemini and NotebookLM are utilised, regardless of the type of data that may be input.

Use of other licenced GenAI tools is not prohibited, but such tools must be procured in accordance with any applicable procurement policy or process, including but not limited to the completion of any requisite risk assessments such as DPIAs and/or ISRAs.

The public, free versions of Copilot, Gemini and NotebookLM, available via a web browser, must not be used for University activities and purposes as they do not guarantee a sufficient level of information security or confidentiality.

In the limited circumstances where a formal risk assessment is required, the University Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and Information Security Risk Assessment (ISRA) processes remain the relevant risk assessments processes to follow.

heldClaims.text: Historical IS&T guidance captured on May 6, 2026: MIT prohibits the use of generative AI for purposes that may require in-depth risk assessments without prior consultation with ai-guidance@mit.edu. Such purposes include recruitment and hiring of employees, evaluating student academic performance, making investment decisions, and complaint and dispute resolution. This specific provision is not reproduced on the current guidance page; its current applicability has not been confirmed.

Historical IS&T guidance captured on May 6, 2026: MIT departments, labs, centers, and institutes (DLCIs) already using a generative AI tool or service must ensure that the tool complies with all Institute policies and Information Protection guidelines, and must contact ai-guidance@mit.edu for consultation or assessment if needed. This specific provision is not reproduced on the current guidance page; its current applicability has not been confirmed.

topics.title: Disclosure
topics.summary: ETH Zurich's declaration of originality provides two options: confirming that no generative AI was used, or confirming that authorised generative AI was used and its disclosure agreed with the supervisor. Bachelor's and Master's theses require a signed declaration of originality, while requirements for other written assessments depend on the applicable academic instructions. Doctoral candidates declare independent authorship through the doctoral examination registration process. The permitted use, disclosure format and any exceptions must follow the relevant supervisor and unit requirements. ETH Zurich's teaching guidelines instruct students to be transparent about their use of generative AI and to identify which tools contributed to which parts of their work, in accordance with applicable lecturer instructions and citation conventions. For scientific writing and theses, students should agree in advance with their supervisors on authorised AI use and disclosure requirements. ETH Library guidance recognises an exception where a supervisor has expressly agreed that particular AI use need not be separately declared. In the absence of such an agreement, undeclared use may constitute a breach of academic integrity.

topics.title: Research & publication
topics.summary: Researchers and students are fully responsible for the integrity of their scientific work and must verify AI-generated output, references, and facts. Generative AI tools cannot be listed as authors or cited as authoritative sources. Theses require signed originality declarations; doctoral candidates declare independent authorship upon registration for the doctoral examination. Researchers must comply with applicable funder (e.g. SNSF) and publisher guidelines.

claims.text: Generative AI and assessments | Students - UCL

evidence.quote:

topics.title: Disclosure
topics.summary: ETH Zurich's declaration of originality provides two options: confirming that no generative AI was used, or confirming that authorised generative AI was used and its disclosure agreed with the supervisor. Bachelor's and Master's theses require a signed declaration of originality, while requirements for other written assessments depend on the applicable academic instructions. Doctoral candidates declare independent authorship through the doctoral examination registration process. The permitted use, disclosure format and any exceptions must follow the relevant supervisor and unit requirements. ETH Zurich's teaching guidelines instruct students to be transparent about their use of generative AI and to identify which tools contributed to which parts of their work, in accordance with applicable lecturer instructions and citation conventions. For scientific writing and theses, students should agree in advance with their supervisors on authorised AI use and disclosure requirements. ETH Library guidance recognises an exception where a supervisor has expressly agreed that particular AI use need not be separately declared. In the absence of such an agreement, undeclared use may constitute a breach of academic integrity.

topics.title: Research & publication
topics.summary: Researchers and students are fully responsible for the integrity of their scientific work and must verify AI-generated output, references, and facts. Generative AI tools cannot be listed as authors or cited as authoritative sources. Theses require signed originality declarations; doctoral candidates declare independent authorship upon registration for the doctoral examination. Researchers must comply with applicable funder (e.g. SNSF) and publisher guidelines.

additionalTopics.title: Academic integrity
additionalTopics.summary: ETH Library provides Turnitin Originality to eligible professors and lecturers for text-similarity checking, subject to data classification and responsible selective-use guidance. Only public or internal documents may be uploaded. claims.claimText: ETH Library guidance requires researchers to remain responsible for their scientific work and to verify AI-generated information, references and quotations. Generative AI tools cannot be listed as scientific authors or relied upon as authoritative scientific sources. Researchers should agree on permitted AI use with collaborators and follow applicable departmental, funder, publisher and journal requirements. Disclosure of an AI tool's contribution is distinct from citing that tool as evidence for a scientific claim.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: In terms of external page copyright law (Article 2), this does not constitute a new work, which is why these tools cannot be considered as authors or co-authors. AI Tools & Licenses
This page provides an overview of common generative AI tools, a field that is constantly growing and changing. The use of Microsoft Copilot as well as Google Gemini and NotebookLM is currently recommended, as data-protected access is possible directly via an ETH account.
The scope of application of AI goes far beyond the tools listed here. The ETH AI Center is working intensively on

various application scenarios, including in the field of teaching, and is the central hub for artificial intelligence. Some possibilities of application in the field of teaching, which are currently being developed, are listed under projects . You can also find specific information on the direct use of these tools under Assistance for Teaching .
Apertus
(Image: EPFL, ETH Zurich, CSCS / Molinari Design)
The language model external page Apertus was developed in collaboration between ETH Zurich, EPFL, and CSCS (Swiss National Supercomputing Center). It serves as a foundation on which developers and organizations can build future applications, such as chatbots, translation systems, and digital l

earning tools.
The entire development process, including architecture, model weights, training data, and methods, is freely accessible and comprehensively documented. Initial impressions of the multilingual model can be gained via the test platform external page Try Apertus . Detailed information about the project can be found on the website of the external page Swiss AI Initiative .
Recommended generative AI tools
The page on AI-Tools at ETH Zurich provides an up-to-date overview of the growing landscape of various AI tools. The Gemini and NotebookLM offerings from Google, as well as Copilot from Microsoft, which are accessible via an ETH cloud subscription, are available to all ETH employe

es and students via secure access. It is therefore recommended that these tools be used primarily for teaching purposes.
Status, October 2025
The external page Microsoft Copilot Website (formerly Bing Chat) is a tool based on generative AI that can generate text and images and is available free of charge. The service can be accessed in a protected environment via a Microsoft 365 Cloud Subscription , which is provided by ETH Zürich.
In addition to direct web access, Copilot is also integrated directly into the Edge browser and can also be used via your ETH account. An overview of the entire product range (including M365 Copilot and Github Copilot) is available on the website Microsoft Copilot

from IT Services.
The freely accessible version of Microsoft Copilot offers
freely available text and image generation,
the ‘ protected ’ status (with Microsoft ETH-account ), whereby personal data is not used as training data,
a chat history of previously executed queries,
the direct integration of an Internet search,
links to further resources,
uploading a document for specific questioning.
The fee-based Pro/Business versions offer
prioritised access,
GPTs that can be configured for your own needs (‘chat bots’),
the integration of Copilot into office and other Microsoft applications.
The licence cost for Copilot for M365 is charged on a per-user, per-year basis. All details on the specifi

c and technical information can be found at Microsoft Copilot , the offer overview page of Cloud Services at ETH Zurich.
Status, October 2025
The offering external page Google Gemini (formerly Bard) is based on a Large Language Model (LLM) developed by Google itself. It can be used, among other things, to integrate image uploads and voice input to generate texts.
ETH Zurich offers a Google Workspace Cloud Subscription that allows the service to be used free of charge and in a protected environment. As with Microsoft Copilot, data entered is not used to train the models.
The free version of Google Gemini offers
free text generation based on text, image or voice input,
a protected status (with

Google ETH account ), whereby personal data is not used by Google as training data,
direct integration of an internet search,
the chat history of previously executed queries.
The advanced version, which is subject to a fee, offers
prioritised access and more up-to-date models,
direct integration of personal data storage.
All the specific details about the ETH Google account in connection with Google Gemini and the associated options can be found at Google AI Tools from ETH Zurich's cloud services.
Status, July 2025
The external page NotebookLM application from Google enables users to work and interact with their own resources. It is characterized by a wide range of possible uses. In additio

n, a customized podcast can be created that provides alternative access to the content provided.
Notebooks can be shared within ETH Zurich. This enables access to resources within groups or for students as part of learning units.
As with Google Gemini, ETH Zurich offers access via the Google Workspace Cloud subscription . This guarantees the use of the service in a protected environment in which the data entered is not used for training the models.
The free version of NotebookLM offers
the ability to upload your own documents and link to websites,
create summaries and interact with content,
and generate podcasts.
The paid Pro version offers
expanded resource integration,
access to newer mode

ls,
and advanced customisation options.
Further information on the offerings can be found at Google AI Tools in the ETH Zurich IT knowledge database.
Additional AI tools
The following non-exhaustive list shows a selection of these tools that are currently well known or have proven to be particularly useful.
Status, December 2024
OpenAI was the first player on the market with external page ChatGPT and was able to establish itself across the board very quickly. The further development of the Large Language Models (LLM), the refinement of the options for interacting with the model and the range of products on offer are constantly expanding.
With the introduction of GPTs (custom GPTs, personal ‘

chat bots’) in autumn 2023, it also became possible to enhance the outputs of generative AI with your own data and configure them to suit your own needs. This offer is subject to certain restrictions and in some cases is only possible via the paid Plus version.
The freely accessible version of ChaptGPT offers
freely available text generation,
a chat history of previously executed queries ( note : data is stored on the OpenAI server).
The Plus/Team versions, which are subject to a charge, offer
prioritised access and more up-to-date models,
image generation,
GPTs (‘chat bots’) that can be configured for your own needs.
A personal account must always be created to access ChatGPT. It is strongl

y recommended to switch off the option "Improve the model for everyone" so that inserted texts and data are not used for training the model (see external page Data Controls FAQ von OpenAI).
Status, December 2024
Anthropic, the company behind the product external page Claude.AI , has made a name for itself in recent months with its highly advanced Large Language Model (LLM). This product also allows users to upload images and integrate multiple documents (upload limit in the free version).
The freely accessible version of Claude.AI offers
freely available text generation based on text,
upload of your own documents,
a chat history of previously executed queries ( note : data is stored on the s

erver).
The chargeable Pro-/Team-version offers
prioritised access and more up-to-date models,
organisation of projects as well as document mangament.
In order to access Claude.AI, a personal account must be created in any case. Anthropic guarantees that the data used for the interaction with the LLM will not be used to train their models (see Anthropic's external page Data Handling & Retention ).
Below is a list of some AI tools that are currently also frequently used and supplement the tools above. The list does not claim to be exhaustive.
external page Perplexity AI focusses on correct references to further resources.
external page DeepSeek and external page Grok are other well known and

often discussed GenAI tools.
external page There's an AI for That offers a search engine for every conceivable AI tool.
A number of AI-based tools have already become established, particularly in scientific work and literature research. A brief overview can be found here.
Connected Papers is a literature research tool (premium version via the ETH Zurich account).
Scopus AI and Scite , AI-powered research tools available at ETH Zurich.
external page Open Knowledge Maps , an AI-based search engine for science.
external page ResearchRabbit provides support in organising and searching for literature.
Information security and artificial intelligence
In order to make targeted but also responsible

use of the possibilities offered by generative AI technologies while minimizing risks such as data protection violations and ethical conflicts, IT Services Information Security has published guidelines for the safe use of AI at ETH Zurich .
The protection of sensitive and personal data is a top priority. In addition, it is important to always keep an eye on the critical review of content and compliance with legal frameworks.

Plagiarism check
Plagiarism check
Please note that access to the plagiarism detection software is exclusively intended for professors and lecturers of ETH Zurich. Students and employees without the lecturer role cannot use Turnitin Originality.
(Access to Turnitin Originality (with ETH account))
Turnitin Originality is a web-based text similarity detectio

n software. Submitted documents are compared against an extensive database of academic papers (both published and unpublished), books, journals, and other sources:
Some features:
Doc-to-doc comparison: direct comparison of a document with one or up to 5 other documents.
Detecting plagiarism: Turnitin Originality detects similarities in texts including paraphrasing, citations and references.
Originality reports: The tool generates an originality report that highlights all the areas of the document that match the sources in the database. The report also shows the percentage of similarity and the matching sources.
Checking quotations and references: Turnitin Originality can check citations and

references in submitted documents to ensure that they are properly formatted and incorporated correctly.
There are a few things to keep in mind when using Turnitin Originality:
Note the confidentiality level: Only documents classified as "public" or "internal" may be uploaded to Turnitin Originality for similarity checking. For more details, see the Download terms and conditions of use (PDF, 143 KB) .
Understand the limitations: Turnitin Originality is not infallible. It relies on its source database and may not detect all instances of plagiarism, for example, if the source is not in the database. Turnitin Originality is not a substitute for teaching proper citation and referencing practices

. Instructors should guide students on correct citation and referencing. Here, the ETH Library offers support.
Watch out for false positives: Turnitin Originality can mark text as plagiarised even if it is properly cited. It is important to carefully review the flagged text to determine if it is indeed plagiarised or a false positive.
False positives: Turnitin Originality may flag sections of texts as plagiarised even if they have been cited correctly. Always check highlighted sections carefully to determine if they have really been plagiarised or if the software has merely produced a false positive.
Use the software responsibly: Plagiarism detection software should be used in a responsible

and ethical manner. Selective use only in cases of suspicion prevents a culture of mistrust. The following use cases are possible: Plagiarism check of written work of students from the teaching context such as term papers and bachelor's/master's theses: The plagiarism check is carried out by supervisors (usually professors or lecturers) if plagiarism is suspected. If the suspicion is confirmed, it is communicated by the supervisors to the ETH's Office of Legal Affairs in Teaching and further processed together with them. Plagiarism check of written work that is produced in the context of a doctorate: Term papers, papers, abstracts, doctoral theses. The examination is carried out by superviso

rs (professors or lecturers) if plagiarism is suspected. If the suspicion is confirmed, it will be communicated by the supervisors to the ETH Research Ethics via trusted persons and followed up. Plagiarism check of texts produced in the context of research: Papers, abstracts, habilitation theses, etc. The check is carried out by members of the department (mostly professors or lecturers) if plagiarism is suspected. If the suspicion is confirmed: proceed as described in the previous point.

AI Tools & Licenses
This page provides an overview of common generative AI tools, a field that is constantly growing and changing. The use of Microsoft Copilot as well as Google Gemini and NotebookLM is currently recommended, as data-protected access is possible directly via an ETH account.
The scope of application of AI goes far beyond the tools listed here. The ETH AI Center is working intensively on

various application scenarios, including in the field of teaching, and is the central hub for artificial intelligence. Some possibilities of application in the field of teaching, which are currently being developed, are listed under projects . You can also find specific information on the direct use of these tools under Assistance for Teaching .
Apertus
(Image: EPFL, ETH Zurich, CSCS / Molinari Design)
The language model external page Apertus was developed in collaboration between ETH Zurich, EPFL, and CSCS (Swiss National Supercomputing Center). It serves as a foundation on which developers and organizations can build future applications, such as chatbots, translation systems, and digital l

earning tools.
The entire development process, including architecture, model weights, training data, and methods, is freely accessible and comprehensively documented. Initial impressions of the multilingual model can be gained via the test platform external page Try Apertus . Detailed information about the project can be found on the website of the external page Swiss AI Initiative .
Recommended generative AI tools
The page on AI-Tools at ETH Zurich provides an up-to-date overview of the growing landscape of various AI tools. The Gemini and NotebookLM offerings from Google, as well as Copilot from Microsoft, which are accessible via an ETH cloud subscription, are available to all ETH employe

es and students via secure access. It is therefore recommended that these tools be used primarily for teaching purposes.
Status, October 2025
The external page Microsoft Copilot Website (formerly Bing Chat) is a tool based on generative AI that can generate text and images and is available free of charge. The service can be accessed in a protected environment via a Microsoft 365 Cloud Subscription , which is provided by ETH Zürich.
In addition to direct web access, Copilot is also integrated directly into the Edge browser and can also be used via your ETH account. An overview of the entire product range (including M365 Copilot and Github Copilot) is available on the website Microsoft Copilot

from IT Services.
The freely accessible version of Microsoft Copilot offers
freely available text and image generation,
the ‘ protected ’ status (with Microsoft ETH-account ), whereby personal data is not used as training data,
a chat history of previously executed queries,
the direct integration of an Internet search,
links to further resources,
uploading a document for specific questioning.
The fee-based Pro/Business versions offer
prioritised access,
GPTs that can be configured for your own needs (‘chat bots’),
the integration of Copilot into office and other Microsoft applications.
The licence cost for Copilot for M365 is charged on a per-user, per-year basis. All details on the specifi

c and technical information can be found at Microsoft Copilot , the offer overview page of Cloud Services at ETH Zurich.
Status, October 2025
The offering external page Google Gemini (formerly Bard) is based on a Large Language Model (LLM) developed by Google itself. It can be used, among other things, to integrate image uploads and voice input to generate texts.
ETH Zurich offers a Google Workspace Cloud Subscription that allows the service to be used free of charge and in a protected environment. As with Microsoft Copilot, data entered is not used to train the models.
The free version of Google Gemini offers
free text generation based on text, image or voice input,
a protected status (with

Google ETH account ), whereby personal data is not used by Google as training data,
direct integration of an internet search,
the chat history of previously executed queries.
The advanced version, which is subject to a fee, offers
prioritised access and more up-to-date models,
direct integration of personal data storage.
All the specific details about the ETH Google account in connection with Google Gemini and the associated options can be found at Google AI Tools from ETH Zurich's cloud services.
Status, July 2025
The external page NotebookLM application from Google enables users to work and interact with their own resources. It is characterized by a wide range of possible uses. In additio

n, a customized podcast can be created that provides alternative access to the content provided.
Notebooks can be shared within ETH Zurich. This enables access to resources within groups or for students as part of learning units.
As with Google Gemini, ETH Zurich offers access via the Google Workspace Cloud subscription . This guarantees the use of the service in a protected environment in which the data entered is not used for training the models.
The free version of NotebookLM offers
the ability to upload your own documents and link to websites,
create summaries and interact with content,
and generate podcasts.
The paid Pro version offers
expanded resource integration,
access to newer mode

ls,
and advanced customisation options.
Further information on the offerings can be found at Google AI Tools in the ETH Zurich IT knowledge database.
Additional AI tools
The following non-exhaustive list shows a selection of these tools that are currently well known or have proven to be particularly useful.
Status, December 2024
OpenAI was the first player on the market with external page ChatGPT and was able to establish itself across the board very quickly. The further development of the Large Language Models (LLM), the refinement of the options for interacting with the model and the range of products on offer are constantly expanding.
With the introduction of GPTs (custom GPTs, personal ‘

chat bots’) in autumn 2023, it also became possible to enhance the outputs of generative AI with your own data and configure them to suit your own needs. This offer is subject to certain restrictions and in some cases is only possible via the paid Plus version.
The freely accessible version of ChaptGPT offers
freely available text generation,
a chat history of previously executed queries ( note : data is stored on the OpenAI server).
The Plus/Team versions, which are subject to a charge, offer
prioritised access and more up-to-date models,
image generation,
GPTs (‘chat bots’) that can be configured for your own needs.
A personal account must always be created to access ChatGPT. It is strongl

y recommended to switch off the option "Improve the model for everyone" so that inserted texts and data are not used for training the model (see external page Data Controls FAQ von OpenAI).
Status, December 2024
Anthropic, the company behind the product external page Claude.AI , has made a name for itself in recent months with its highly advanced Large Language Model (LLM). This product also allows users to upload images and integrate multiple documents (upload limit in the free version).
The freely accessible version of Claude.AI offers
freely available text generation based on text,
upload of your own documents,
a chat history of previously executed queries ( note : data is stored on the s

erver).
The chargeable Pro-/Team-version offers
prioritised access and more up-to-date models,
organisation of projects as well as document mangament.
In order to access Claude.AI, a personal account must be created in any case. Anthropic guarantees that the data used for the interaction with the LLM will not be used to train their models (see Anthropic's external page Data Handling & Retention ).
Below is a list of some AI tools that are currently also frequently used and supplement the tools above. The list does not claim to be exhaustive.
external page Perplexity AI focusses on correct references to further resources.
external page DeepSeek and external page Grok are other well known and

often discussed GenAI tools.
external page There's an AI for That offers a search engine for every conceivable AI tool.
A number of AI-based tools have already become established, particularly in scientific work and literature research. A brief overview can be found here.
Connected Papers is a literature research tool (premium version via the ETH Zurich account).
Scopus AI and Scite , AI-powered research tools available at ETH Zurich.
external page Open Knowledge Maps , an AI-based search engine for science.
external page ResearchRabbit provides support in organising and searching for literature.
Information security and artificial intelligence
In order to make targeted but also responsible

use of the possibilities offered by generative AI technologies while minimizing risks such as data protection violations and ethical conflicts, IT Services Information Security has published guidelines for the safe use of AI at ETH Zurich .
The protection of sensitive and personal data is a top priority. In addition, it is important to always keep an eye on the critical review of content and compliance with legal frameworks.

AI Tools at ETH Zurich
This page is only available in English.
Safe use of AI Before exploring the capabilities of these tools, follow our Information Security Guidelines to ensure compliance with ETH Zurich’s data protection and security standards. Review the official recommendations here . Users are responsible for using AI tools in an authorized and responsible manner. See Guide for Users of AI at ETH Zurich . Uploading strictly confidential data to external cloud services, including AI tools, is prohibited. The work mode of M365 Copilot without the web search option is approved for use with confidential

data . The web search option is disabled in the work mode by default. M365 Copilot Chat and the web mode of M365 Copilot is approved for internal data . AI tools lacking a cloud assessment have not been released for use with ETH data. Processing confidential, strictly confidential, or protected personal data is not permitted. AI‑generated output must be reviewed before use.
Data classification Information owners classify the information according to the risk-oriented approach as explained in RSETHZ 203.28 Appendix 1a Information is classified as “ strictly confidential ” if unauthorised access could damage the interests of ETH Zurich. It must not be stored on external cloud services and may

only be shared with a specifically authorised group under strict security precautions. Information is classified as “ confidential ” if unauthorised access could significantly damage the interests of ETH Zurich. It must be limited to specific authorised individuals and securely stored. Information is classified as “ internal ” if unauthorised access could damage the interests of ETH Zurich. Such information is therefore generally intended solely for members of ETH Zurich. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, all data and information at ETH is considered “internal”. Information is considered public if it is authorized for publication by the responsible body. additionalTopics.title: Teaching guidance
additionalTopics.summary: Prior approval is required through the AI System for Assurance and Evaluation before deploying AI to provide instruction, feedback, or marks (Section 2.4). Spot checks should still be conducted even where AI scoring is considered reliable.

claims.claimText: NUS policy sets the default assumption that AI tool use is permitted for unsupervised (take-home) assessments with due acknowledgement; if an assessment forbids AI for pedagogical reasons, crucial aspects of that assessment should be conducted in person and under instructor supervision.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
If the decision is that students should be forbidden from using AI tools for an assessment (for
pedagogical reasons), then crucial aspects of that assessment should be conducted in person
and under instructor supervision, to ensure that students do not access those tools.

Conversely, the default assumption for any unsupervised (e.g., “take-home”) assessment task
is that the use of AI tools is permitted so long as the use is duly acknowledged.

claims.text: Generative AI and assessments | Students - UCL

evidence.quote:
For Category 1, you might use GenAI tools to help you revise and prepare, but the work you complete for the assessment should be your own.
In Category 2, you could use GenAI to get ideas, help draft your work, or even proofread what you've written. Just make sure you keep a note of how you've used GenAI, so that you can acknowledge it afterwards. You won't lose marks just for having used GenAI.
Category 3 is a lot like category 2, but there will also be some essential use of GenAI as part of the assessment.

topics.title: Disclosure
topics.summary: Acknowledgement is required whenever GenAI has been used as a functional tool to assist in creating academic work (drafting, planning, structuring). Minimum acknowledgement requires tool name/version, publisher, URL, and single-sentence context. Where required by standard referencing styles (APA, Chicago) or departmental guidelines, the GenAI tool may be cited as an author in addition to functional acknowledgement.

Name and version of the GenAI system used; e.g. Microsoft Copilot (version GPT-4); ChatGPT-3.5

claims.claimText: UCL Library guidance requires acknowledgement where GenAI has functionally contributed to the creation of academic work (e.g. drafting, planning, structuring), subject to discipline and assessment instructions. Minimum acknowledgement includes tool name and version, publisher, URL, and single-sentence context of use. Prompts, generation dates, and tracked-changes are additional requirements that apply only when stipulated by departments or assignment briefs. Preparatory reading, search summaries, and basic grammar assistance may not require acknowledgement. While UCL advises treating AI output as a work with no author, students and researchers must follow required departmental guidelines and standardised referencing styles (such as APA or Chicago), which may require citing the GenAI tool as an author.

evidence.evidenceSnippet:
A GenAI tool cannot be classed as an author – it cannot take responsibility for its work, nor does it generate original ideas but reproduces ideas found elsewhere.
A primary function of a reference list is so the reader can refer to the original source, which is not possible with AI generated content.

claims.claimText: UCL does not invest in GenAI detection software. Staff must not submit student work into GenAI detection tools or GenAI services themselves, as this compromises students' intellectual property and personal data rights. Furthermore, due to lack of evidence that GenAI can mark effectively and without bias, staff should not use GenAI to mark student work. UCL markers do not use AI detector scores to establish academic misconduct. Initial informal discussions do not replace the formal Student Academic Misconduct Procedure; suspected inappropriate GenAI use or authorship issues may proceed through Stage 1 and an Investigatory Viva.

claims.claimText: For an Investigatory Viva, the Secretary must supply the invitation, report and evidence at least five working days beforehand. Attendance is mandatory and the viva cannot be held in the student’s absence. Organisation should occur within 20 working days of the Stage 1 outcome unless reasonable circumstances prevent this. claims.claimText: CLIE oral and invigilated in-person assessments are Category 1 unless otherwise stated; non-invigilated written assessments are Category 2 with assistive use only. CLIE Modern Foreign Language modules prohibit language and writing review. Summer School rules are set by the teaching department. CLIE requires acknowledgement of GenAI use.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: CLIE’s policy is based on UCL’s three categories of GenAI use in assessment. CLIE oral assessments and invigilated in-person assessments are category 1 unless otherwise stated: generative AI tools cannot be used. This is because the use of generative AI is wholly inappropriate for the skills to be assessed and the format in which they are assessed.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: UCL staff and students can now access Microsoft Copilot. Microsoft Copilot is a safer generative AI tool than using the consumer-oriented generative AI services, provided you log in with your UCL credentials.

Microsoft Copilot is our approved GenAI tool because of its enhanced data protection. This tool is a more secure and safer alternative to other GenAI services. Read about how you can use Microsoft Copilot easily and safely.
If you sign into Microsoft Copilot with your UCL credentials you can be confident that:
your prompts, questions and results are protected
the chat data is not saved
Microsoft has no eyes-on access.
This means no one can view your data and your data is not used to train the AI models.

Microsoft Copilot is grounded in data from the public web and provides verifiable answers with citations, along with visual answers that include graphs and charts. It is designed in line with Microsoft’s AI principles.

tools.description: Formative academic writing, structure and referencing feedback; not substantive assessment text or academic credit.
tools.howToObtain: Access through UCL Moodle. Available 24/7 with unlimited uses for current UCL students.
tools.costToUser: Not verified in the reviewed evidence.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Studiosity can review your work and give you feedback to help improve the structure, language, spelling and grammar, and use of sources in your writing. This service is available 24/7 and there is no limit to the number of times you can use it.

This means that, unlike other AI tools, you can use Studiosity with confidence that it is supporting your learning. Studiosity, uses a ‘closed system’ AI, so your work remains your own and will not be used to train AI.
All current UCL students can access Studiosity via Moodle, where you'll also find frequently asked questions and links to further resources

UCL is the Controller of your personal data for the purposes of providing academic skills support. Studiosity Pty Ltd (Studiosity) acts as a Processor when providing services on behalf of UCL. Additionally, Studiosity acts as an independent Controller for data collected directly from you to manage your user account and platform improvements.

Your personal data is processed by Studiosity in Australia and the United States. To ensure your data receives an adequate level of protection, these transfers are governed by the UK Approved International Data Transfer Addendum.†ico.org.uk
* Service Content: Submitted academic drafts for feedback, "Connect Live" session transcripts (including audio recordings), and chat histories.

We have put in place appropriate security measures to prevent data loss or unauthorized access. This includes AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2+ encryption in transit, and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for administrative access. We retain your data only as long as necessary to fulfill the purposes of the service or as required by the UCL Records Retention Schedule .

You may not use generative AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Copilot, Colab’s built-in AI) in this course.

scope.en: In HSS, use AI only as explicitly allowed by the instructor in the course materials; assume other uses are disallowed. Bi 1 rules are course-specific. Admissions rules concern applications; tool access does not approve assessment or sensitive-data use.

do.en: Check the exact assignment and audience.

do.en: Follow disclosure instructions and applicable exceptions.

do.en: Check data classification and tool mode.

dont.en: Do not infer assessment permission from tool access.

dont.zh: 不要把课程或出版社规则推广到全校。

additionalTopics.title: Academic integrity

claims.text: HKU TALIC guidance identifies misuse of AI or misrepresentation of AI work as independent creative work as violations of HKU regulations, with referral to the university disciplinary committee. This statement does not establish an automatic sanction.

evidence.quote: ANY misuse of AI or misrepresentation of AI work as one’s own independent creative work violates the HKU regulations as well as generally accepted principles of community, integrity and honor. Violations will be referred to the university disciplinary committee.

claims.text: HKU Faculty of Law requires students to declare AI use on its assignment cover sheet where a teacher permits it for an assignment; failure to declare is treated as academic misconduct akin to plagiarism.

evidence.quote: In addition, the Faculty’s assignment cover sheet requires students to declare their use of AI tools, where this is permitted by a teacher for the purposes of an assignment. Failure to do so constitutes academic misconduct akin to plagiarism, and will be treated in the same manner.
evidence.title: Policy and Guidelines – Course Profile
evidence.location: Plagiarism and the Misuse of Generative and other AI tools in assessment; normalized_extracted_text; quote characters 2522–2804; part 1/1.

claims.text: For HKU Faculty of Law assessed work, an educative response may involve rewriting and resubmission with a penalty. Where this is not appropriate, an academic response may reduce the mark or give zero. Misuse may also be referred as a disciplinary offence; this is not automatic expulsion.

evidence.quote: When a teacher is satisfied that submitted work contains plagiarism or involves the misuse of generative and other AI tools, and that an educative response (usually involving re-writing and re-submission with a penalty) is not appropriate, then an academic response will be adopted, pursuant to which the plagiarized work may be given a mark of zero or a reduced mark. In addition, the matter may be treated as a disciplinary offence (just like the case of cheating during an examination) and referred to the University’s Disciplinary Committee under Statute XXXI of the University’s Statutes and the Disciplinary Committee Regulations.

claims.claimText: For HKU Faculty of Law assessed work, an educative response may involve rewriting and resubmission with a penalty. Where this is not appropriate, an academic response may reduce the mark or give zero. Misuse may also be referred as a disciplinary offence; this is not automatic expulsion.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: When a teacher is satisfied that submitted work contains plagiarism or involves the misuse of generative and other AI tools, and that an educative response (usually involving re-writing and re-submission with a penalty) is not appropriate, then an academic response will be adopted, pursuant to which the plagiarized work may be given a mark of zero or a reduced mark. In addition, the matter may be treated as a disciplinary offence (just like the case of cheating during an examination) and referred to the University’s Disciplinary Committee under Statute XXXI of the University’s Statutes and the Disciplinary Committee Regulations.

title.en: Check the task rules and research conditions.

scope.en: Follow assessment instructions, declare permitted assistance and protect data. Research and Faculty of Law requirements have distinct scopes.

heldClaims.text: NTU guidelines state that AI detector tools should be used with caution due to frequent false positives and negatives, ease of bypass, and bias against non-native English writing patterns.

topics.title: Coursework
topics.summary: NTU’s 2025 statement generally permits assignment AI use, with teacher prohibitions for pedagogical reasons. Current Library guidance requires module instructions and explicit permission for extensive use.
topics.scope: Dated institutional statement and current Library guidance; internal full teaching policy not obtained.

claims.text: NTU’s dated 24 June 2025 statement says GenAI is generally permitted in assignments, but professors may prohibit it for specific pedagogical reasons communicated to students. Students are expected to declare use and how it was used, and remain responsible for accuracy and citations. This is a dated institutional statement, not the complete current internal teaching policy or permission for every assessment.

evidence.quote: NTU’s policy is that in general, students are allowed to use Gen AI in their assignments. Many Schools across STEM and non-STEM disciplines, in medicine, and at NIE, are already using AI as part of learning. Students are expected to declare any use of AI, and how they are being used. When using AI, students are ultimately responsible for the content generated. They must ensure factual accuracy and cite all sources properly. Some professors may prohibit Gen AI for certain assignments for specific pedagogical reasons. In such cases, the reason for disallowing it is clearly communicated to students.
evidence.title: Comment on the use of AI in education | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: Official statement, 24 June 2025; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 9338:9941

claims.text: NTU Library advises students to check instructor and assignment instructions before using AI because expectations vary by module and discipline.

evidence.quote: Expectations around AI use may vary by module and discipline; seek clarification from your instructor or refer to assignment instructions before use.
evidence.title: Guidelines for Responsible Use - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Consult; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 572:721

claims.text: NTU Library instructs students to obtain explicit instructor permission for more extensive AI involvement, such as generating source materials or enhancing visuals.

evidence.quote: Obtain explicit permission from your instructor for more extensive AI involvement, such as generating source materials or enhancing visuals.
evidence.title: Introduction - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Key Points on Ethical AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 3124:3264

topics.title: Exams
topics.summary: Do not access AI during exams where external resources are forbidden. Check the exact examination instructions; open-resource exams do not automatically authorise AI.
topics.scope: NTU Library guidance; restriction applies when external resources are not permitted.

claims.text: NTU Library instructs students not to access AI tools during examinations when external resources are not permitted. This condition does not establish either a ban in every exam or automatic AI permission in open-resource exams.

evidence.quote: Follow Exam Protocols. Do not access AI tools during examinations when external resources are not permitted to maintain fair testing conditions.
evidence.title: Guidelines for Responsible Use - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Consult, Follow Exam Protocols; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 722:866

topics.title: Disclosure
topics.statusLabel: Disclose use; check the required detail
topics.summary: Disclose AI assistance in submissions and follow module requirements. Detailed prompt/output records and the format depend on the instructor; thesis submissions have a separate Statement of Originality requirement.
topics.scope: Student Library guidance; separate thesis submission declarations.

claims.text: NTU Library instructs students to disclose AI-tool use in their submissions and follow their module’s AI-use policy and instructor guidance. The required level of documentation and disclosure format depend on the assignment and instructor’s expectations; detailed prompt-and-output records and a particular declaration form are not universal requirements.

evidence.quote: Use AI tools to support tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, or checking grammar, but ensure you disclose their use in your submissions. Always refer to your module's AI use policy and seek guidance from your instructor regarding specific expectations for acceptable AI usage in your courses.
evidence.title: Introduction - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Key Points on Ethical AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 2828:3123

evidence.quote: When using AI for assignments (e.g., grammar checks, copyediting, or idea generation), adhere to the specific guidelines set by your instructor, as expectations may vary by module and discipline. This may include documenting your AI use, completing a “ Declaration on GAI Use ,” or disclosing AI contributions where required. To uphold academic integrity, you must always provide proper citations for all sources used, including AI‑generated content.
evidence.title: Document, Disclose & Cite AI Usage - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Purpose of Documenting, Disclosing and Citing AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 674:1124

claims.text: For some assignments, instructors may require AI process records. NTU Library’s tracking template may be used or adapted when record-keeping is required or recommended, following the instructor’s format and level of detail.

evidence.quote: For some course assignments, instructors may require you to document your AI use. This supports transparency in your learning process and clarifies how AI was used at different stages of your work. Such records may be submitted as an appendix. To support this, NTU Library provides a ready‑to‑use template that outlines what to document. This template may be used or adapted when record‑keeping is required or recommended, while following your instructor’s preferred format and level of detail.
evidence.title: Document, Disclose & Cite AI Usage - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Document AI Usage (When Required or Recommended); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 1365:1859

claims.text: From November 2025, NTU’s thesis/dissertation Statement of Originality includes an AI-use disclosure section. The required declarations form part of thesis submission requirements; the source does not establish a single faculty-independent template.

evidence.quote: The following 3 statements are to be included in all theses and dissertations by students: ​ Statement of Originality : Certifies that work done and reported is the student's own and has not been previously submitted to another University or Institution. [New (from Nov 2025)] It includes a section on the disclosure of AI-use in the preparation of the thesis/ dissertation.
evidence.title: Theses / Dissertations | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: Submission Requirements, Statement of Originality, new from Nov 2025; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 3416:3790

topics.title: Privacy & sensitive data
topics.summary: Do not upload protected research data to external GenAI unless legal, restricted-access and no-retention conditions are met, plus owner permission where applicable or RCA agreement. The RCA route does not waive the other safeguards.
topics.scope: Research data; not approval of all institutional tools for sensitive coursework.

claims.text: In research, confidential or sensitive information and personal data must not be uploaded to external GenAI platforms unless all applicable conditions are met: compliance with relevant laws and institutional policies; access restricted to authorised study members; no retention of the data in or by the GenAI; and, where applicable, explicit written permission from the data owner or agreement to that GenAI use in the Research Collaboration Agreement.

evidence.quote: Any confidential or sensitive information, and/or personal data must not be uploaded to any external GenAI software, system, or platform unless: The activity does not contravene any applicable laws, regulations, or institutional policies; Access to the GenAI is controlled and restricted to only authorised study members involved in the research; The data is not retained in or by the GenAI; and Where applicable, written permission has been explicitly provided by the data owner, or the use of such GenAI has been agreed upon in the Research Collaboration Agreement (RCA).
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §4 Data Privacy & Confidentiality; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 6791:7364

topics.title: Research & publication
topics.statusLabel: Disclose, verify and preserve research integrity
topics.summary: Acknowledge research use beyond basic spelling/grammar checks, retain human authorship and follow stricter recipient rules. Label and document AI visuals; experimental images have explicit methodology exceptions, not permission to fabricate results.
topics.scope: Research proposals, scholarly outputs and theses; original should/must wording remains in evidence.

claims.text: NTU states that generative AI should not be listed as an author of any paper with NTU affiliation, or as a Principal Investigator, Co-PI, or collaborator in research proposals.

evidence.quote: Therefore, GenAI (e.g. ChatGPT) should not be listed as an author of any paper with an affiliation to NTU; or listed as a Principal Investigator (PI), Co-PI, or collaborator in any research proposals.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §2 Authorship; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 4365:4565

claims.text: NTU research policy states that GenAI use beyond basic spelling and grammar checks should be acknowledged and cited, identifying the tool’s full name and version, purpose and use in research proposals, manuscripts and scholarly works.

evidence.quote: In the interests of transparency and integrity, the use of GenAI beyond basic spelling and grammar checks should be appropriately acknowledged and cited . This would include acknowledging the use of any AI tools in their research proposals, manuscripts, and scholarly works through a statement specifying the tool's full name and version, its purpose of use, and how it was used.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §1 Acknowledging/Declaring the Use of GenAI; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 3334:3713

claims.text: NTU requires AI-generated research images, figures and videos to be clearly labelled and the methods, tools and parameters documented sufficiently for reproducibility.

evidence.quote: All AI-generated images, figures, and videos must be clearly labelled as such. Researchers are required to document the methods, tools, and parameters used to generate these visuals in sufficient detail to ensure reproducibility.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §3(i); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 5457:5686

claims.text: AI-generated research visuals must not be presented as actual experimental data unless AI or AI-assisted tools are an essential component of the research design and/or methodology. Using AI to fabricate images resembling experimental results constitutes serious research misconduct.

evidence.quote: AI-generated images, figures and videos must not be presented as actual experimental data unless AI (or AI-assisted) tools are an essential component of the research design and/or methodology. The use of AI to fabricate images to resemble experimental results constitutes serious research misconduct.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §3(ii); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 5691:5991

claims.text: NTU prohibits substantive AI modification of genuine experimental images unless clearly described in the methodology.

evidence.quote: Similarly, the substantive modification of genuine experimental images using AI tools is prohibited unless clearly described in the methodology.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §3(ii); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 5992:6136

claims.text: When an agency, journal or other receiving party has GenAI rules that differ from NTU research policy, researchers should follow the stricter rules.

evidence.quote: If the proposal, manuscript or other document is being submitted to a agency, journal or other party with rules concerning GenAI that differ from the NTU policy, then the stricter rules should be followed.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore

additionalTopics.title: Academic integrity
additionalTopics.summary: Misrepresenting AI work is academic misconduct in the Library’s handbook summary. Research plagiarism and research-misconduct referral have their own conditions; referral is not guilt or an automatic sanction.
additionalTopics.scope: Public Library summary and separately scoped research misconduct procedure.

claims.text: NTU Library’s public summary of the 2025 Academic Integrity Handbook states that misrepresenting AI-generated content as one’s own work is academic misconduct. The complete internal handbook was not independently obtained.

evidence.quote: AI tools can assist your thinking but should not replace it; misrepresenting AI-generated content as your own work is considered academic misconduct.
evidence.title: Introduction - Using AI Discovery Tools Responsibly - LibGuides at Nanyang Technological University
evidence.location: Key Points on Ethical AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 2678:2827

claims.text: NTU states that not citing or acknowledging the use of generative AI could be considered plagiarism (a form of research misconduct), especially if GenAI was used to generate ideas or for literature reviews.

evidence.quote: Not citing or acknowledging the use of GenAI could be considered plagiarism (i.e. a form of research misconduct ), especially if GenAI was used to generate ideas or for literature reviews.
evidence.title: NTU Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Research | Research | NTU Singapore
evidence.location: §1 Acknowledging/Declaring the Use of GenAI; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 3714:3902

claims.text: The Vice President (Research) reviews the RIO preliminary report and may take appropriate action, decide whether to invite the Provost to appoint a COI for faculty/research staff, or decide whether to refer a student to the Board of Discipline. evidence.quote: 4.4.1 The Vice President (Research) shall review the preliminary investigation report from the RIO, who will then take appropriate action (especially in relation to research staff), or decide whether to invite the Provost to appoint a COI to consider the Allegation/ Complaint under the Framework for Investigation and Disciplinary Proceedings for Faculty and Research Staff, or if the Respondent is a student, decide whether to refer to the Board of Discipline, or take any other appropriate action.

evidence.quote: b) For all work that a student submits for any form of academic credit, AI may not be used, whether with or without attribution, in a way that would constitute academic plagiarism if the AI were a human author whose work was used without attribution . Commentary: The crux of this policy, which applies in any context in which a student submits work for evaluation, is the application of existing academic integrity policies. Thus, some but not all uses of AI in preparing work to submit for a class would violate this default policy. evidence.quote: suggestions—would not violate this default policy. Nor would using AI for proofreading. The principle here is that if AI is performing a task that other technologies (or people) currently perform, and such uses are not a violation of academic integrity, then those uses of AI do not violate the default policy. In contrast, using AI to compose part or all of a paper, or copying or paraphrasing output from AI and passing it off as one’s own writing, would violate this default policy. The same principle applies here: if AI is performing a task that other technologies (or people) currently perform, and such uses are a violation of academic integrity, then those uses of AI do

evidence.quote: violate the default policy. The default policy sweeps more broadly than a prohibition against academic plagiarism, however. A student cannot avoid limits on the use of AI that would otherwise apply by attributing their work to AI. It is not plagiarism to copy or paraphrase another’s work, so long as one properly cites that source. But under the default policy, the use of AI with or without attribution is compared to the use of a human-created source without attribution . Thus, using AI to compose all or part of a paper, even if the use of generative AI is fully documented in properly placed footnotes , is a violation of the default policy.

claims.text: UChicago student guidance requires students to follow the instructor’s rules on when and how AI may be used in coursework. Course policies may differ; students should ask when unclear.

evidence.quote: Always refer to the instructors’ guidance on when and how generative artificial intelligence may be used in course work. additionalTopics.statusLabel: Review the tool and intended use
additionalTopics.summary: Tools handling confidential data require review even when free. Paid tools use Procurement; free research/staff use has specified review conditions. A Risk Acceptance Letter may document agreed risks, not waive compliance prohibitions.

claims.text: At the University of Chicago, generative AI systems, applications, and software products that process, analyze, or move confidential data require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free.

evidence.quote: Generative AI systems, applications, and software products that process, analyze, or move confidential data require a security review before they are acquired, even if the software is free.

claims.text: At the University of Chicago, if a proposed AI tool use exceeds standard risk tolerance but is not prohibited by compliance regulations, a Risk Acceptance Letter may be prepared to document reviewed and accepted risks under specific conditions.

evidence.quote: If the proposed use is not prohibited by compliance regulations but exceeds standard risk tolerance, and the requester still wishes to proceed with the purchase, the request is escalated to senior leadership—the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and Chief Technology Officer (CTO), and the Chief Privacy Officer (CPO)—for guidance. If applicable, Information Assurance may prepare an RAL. An RAL serves as formal acknowledgment by requesting unit leadership that specific, defined risks have been reviewed and are being accepted under documented conditions.
